Stand facing the blackboard. The window is on your right, the door is behind you and the cupboard is on your left. Make a quarter turn clockwise. What do you face now?

Answer: The window.

Stand behind the child and turn together, slowly, the way the clock hands go (to the right). One quarter turn moves you from one wall to the next wall. Say "quarter turn" as you stop. Then set tasks: "From the window, a quarter turn clockwise?" (the door) "From the door?" (the cupboard).
Facing the blackboard again, make a half turn. What do you face? Does it matter which way you turn?

Answer: The door (behind you). It does not matter: a half turn clockwise and a half turn anticlockwise both end facing the door.

A half turn is two quarter turns: blackboard -> window -> door. Now try the other way: blackboard -> cupboard -> door. Same place! A half turn always makes you face the opposite way, like turning round to walk back home.
Facing the blackboard, make a three-quarter turn clockwise. What do you face? Can you get there with a shorter turn?

Answer: The cupboard. A quarter turn anticlockwise also takes you to the cupboard.

Count the quarter turns as you go: 1 (window), 2 (door), 3 (cupboard). Then go back to the blackboard and make one quarter turn the other way: cupboard again. Three quarters one way is the same as one quarter the other way, because together they make a full turn (3 + 1 = 4 quarters).
A spinning top turns and stops facing the same way it started. How much has it turned at least?

Answer: At least one full turn.

A full turn is 4 quarter turns and brings you back to where you started. Let the child make a full turn on the spot, counting the 4 walls: 1, 2, 3, 4 - back to the blackboard. A giant wheel at the mela makes a full turn each time a seat comes back to the bottom.
Which way do the hands of a clock move? Which way do you turn a bottle cap to close it?

Answer: Clock hands move clockwise. To close (tighten) a bottle cap you turn it clockwise; to open it you turn it anticlockwise.

Look at a real clock and trace the path of the second hand with your finger: 12, 1, 2, 3 ... That way is clockwise. The other way is anticlockwise ("anti" means against). Try a bottle, a tap and a jar lid together. Say "righty tighty, lefty loosey" to remember it.
In the playground, North is marked on the wall. Ali faces North and makes a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which way does he face?

Answer: West.

Draw a big compass on the ground with chalk: N at the top, then clockwise E, S, W. Clockwise quarter turns go N -> E -> S -> W -> N. Anticlockwise goes the other way: N -> W -> S -> E -> N. So one quarter turn anticlockwise from North is West. Remember the order with "Never Eat Soggy Wafers" (N, E, S, W clockwise). Let the child stand on the compass and turn.
The minute hand points to 12. After 15 minutes it points to 3. What turn has it made? What turn does it make in 30 minutes and in 45 minutes?

Answer: 15 minutes: a quarter turn. 30 minutes: a half turn (to 6). 45 minutes: a three-quarter turn (to 9). 60 minutes: a full turn.

Divide a paper clock into 4 parts with two lines, 12 to 6 and 3 to 9. Each part is a quarter of the clock, and each quarter is 15 minutes. That is why we say "quarter past" for 15 minutes past the hour. Move the hand and let the child say the turn.
Fold a scrap of paper in half, then in half again, to make a right-angle tester. Where can you find right angles in the classroom?

Answer: Corners of a book, a page, the blackboard, a door, a window, a table top, a tile - all have right angles.

The folded corner is a quarter of a full turn: a RIGHT ANGLE. Fit it into corners: if it fits exactly, the corner is a right angle (a square corner). Ask the child to find 10 right angles and one corner that is NOT a right angle.
Open a door a little, then wide open. Compare each opening with your right-angle tester. What do you notice?

Answer: A small opening makes an angle SMALLER than a right angle. A wide opening can make an angle BIGGER than a right angle.

Angle means amount of turn. Open a pair of scissors or your two arms slowly: the angle grows. Hold the tester in the corner: if the gap is inside the tester, it is smaller; if it goes past the tester, it is bigger. Let the child make angles with two pencils and sort them.
A fielder in a cricket match faces East. He makes a three-quarter turn clockwise to watch the ball. Which way does he face now?

Answer: North.

Count quarter turns clockwise from East: 1 South, 2 West, 3 North. Check with the short way: a three-quarter turn clockwise is the same as a quarter turn anticlockwise, and a quarter turn anticlockwise from East is North. Both ways agree.
Meena faces East. She makes a half turn, then a quarter turn clockwise. Which way does she face?

Answer: North.

Do it one turn at a time. East, half turn: West. West, quarter turn clockwise: North. Let the child act it out and say each direction aloud. Then give a 3-step task: "Face South; quarter turn clockwise; half turn; quarter turn anticlockwise" (West, East, North).
At 3 o'clock the two hands of a clock make a right angle. At what other o'clock time do they make a right angle?

Answer: At 9 o'clock.

At 3 o'clock the minute hand is on 12 and the hour hand on 3: a quarter turn apart, which is a right angle. At 9 o'clock the hour hand is a quarter turn the other way from 12. Show it with a paper clock and the tester. At 1 o'clock the angle is smaller; at 5 o'clock it is bigger; at 6 o'clock the hands make a straight line (a half turn).

Hold a piece of string loosely, then pull it tight. What kind of line does it make each time?

Answer: Loose: a curved line. Pulled tight: a straight line.

A straight line goes the same way all the time and never bends. A curved line keeps changing its way. Let the child walk along a straight chalk line and a curved chalk line in the playground. Then ask them to find 5 straight lines (edge of a door, ruler, window bar) and 5 curved lines (bangle, rim of a plate, a rainbow) at home.
A flagpole, the edge of the floor, and a slide in the park: which line is vertical, which is horizontal and which is slanting?

Answer: The flagpole is vertical. The edge of the floor is horizontal. The slide is slanting.

Horizontal comes from "horizon", where the sky meets the sea: it lies flat. Vertical stands straight up, like a person standing tall. Slanting leans, neither flat nor straight up. Use your arm: hold it flat (horizontal), straight up (vertical), and in between (slanting). Play "Simon says" with the three words.
A farmer builds a fence round his field but leaves a gap. His cow walks out through the gap. Is the fence an open figure or a closed figure?

Answer: An open figure, because it has a gap.

A closed figure has no gap: if you walk along it you come back to the start without jumping. Draw the field with a gap and let the child trace it with a finger - the finger falls off at the gap. Then close the gap: now the cow is trapped inside. Only a closed figure has an inside and an outside.

For a game of kho-kho or "lagori", a big circle is drawn on the ground. Riya is in the middle, Sam is standing on the chalk line and Tara is away from the circle. Who is inside, who is outside, and who is on the boundary?

Answer: Riya is inside, Tara is outside, Sam is on the boundary.

The line itself is the boundary. Draw a closed shape on the floor and play "inside, outside, on the line": call out a word and the child jumps to the right place. On paper, draw dots inside, outside and on a shape and let the child colour them in three colours.
How do you draw a straight line of 8 cm between two dots with a ruler?

Answer: Put the 0 of the ruler on the first dot, lay the ruler along to 8, hold it firmly, and draw along the edge from 0 to 8.

Show it slowly: hold the ruler down with the fingers spread in the middle (not at the edge), keep the pencil touching the edge, and pull the pencil along in one smooth stroke. Then let the child draw lines of 5 cm, 10 cm and 3 cm, and check each other's with the ruler.
Write the capital letters A to Z. Which letters are made of only straight lines? Which have only curved lines? Which have both?

Answer: Only straight: A, E, F, H, I, K, L, M, N, T, V, W, X, Y, Z (15). Only curved: C, O, S (3). Both: B, D, G, J, P, Q, R, U (8).

Write each letter large and trace it with a finger: "straight ... straight" or "curve". Sort them into three columns. Check the total: 15 + 3 + 8 = 26 letters. (Letters can look different in different fonts, so accept a good reason.)
Draw a simple house: a square with a triangle roof sitting on top. How many straight lines do you need?

Answer: 6 straight lines: 4 for the square and 2 slanting lines for the roof (the top of the square is also the bottom of the roof).

Draw it together, one line at a time, and number each line as you draw it: 1, 2, 3, 4 for the square, 5, 6 for the roof. Ask: "Do we need another line under the roof?" No - the top side of the square is already there. Then add a door (3 more lines) and count again: 9.
A kolam or rangoli is often drawn around dots with one long line. When the line comes back to where it started, is the figure open or closed?

Answer: Closed - it has no gap and no loose ends.

Draw a small kolam loop around 4 dots with the child, without lifting the chalk. Show that the line ends where it began. Then draw one that stops early: it is open. Rangoli designs are a beautiful way to practise curved lines and closed figures.
When you write 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8, which numbers use only straight lines? Which use only curved lines?

Answer: Only straight: 1, 4, 7. Only curved: 0, 8. Both straight and curved: 2, 5.

Write each number big on the board and trace it: the child says "straight" or "curved" for every part. The 2 has a curved top and a straight bottom; the 5 has a straight top and a curved belly. Different handwriting can differ, so always ask for the reason.
Is the letter O an open or a closed figure? The letter C? The letter D?

Answer: O is closed. C is open (it has two ends). D is closed.

Trace each letter with a finger. If you get back to the start without lifting, it is closed. The C has a gap on the right, so a little ant could walk in and out. The D is closed and made of one straight line and one curved line.
Raju walks from the gate to the tree in a straight line. Sita walks along a curved path from the gate to the tree. Who walks less?

Answer: Raju. The straight line is the shortest way between two places.

Put two chalk marks on the floor. Join them with a straight string, then lay another string along a curvy path. Straighten the curvy string next to the first one: it is longer. That is why people cut straight across a field when they are in a hurry.
Can you draw a closed figure with only 2 straight lines? With 3? With 1 straight line and 1 curved line?

Answer: 2 straight lines: no, they cannot close up. 3 straight lines: yes, a triangle. 1 straight line and 1 curved line: yes, like a half circle (or the letter D).

Give the child 2 sticks and ask them to make a closed shape: they will find it impossible - there is always a gap. With 3 sticks they make a triangle. Then give a stick and a bent pipe cleaner: they can make a D. So the fewest straight lines for a closed figure with only straight sides is 3.

Outside the temple there are 9 pairs of chappals. How many chappals are there? Count in 2s.

Answer: 18 chappals.

Point to each pair and count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Nine counts, so 9 pairs. Counting in 2s is quicker than counting in 1s. Notice all the numbers are even and end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Now let the child count 13 pairs of socks in 2s (26).
6 children hold up both hands. How many fingers are there? Count in 5s.

Answer: 60 fingers.

Each hand has 5 fingers, and there are 12 hands. Count in 5s, touching each hand: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. The numbers end in 5, 0, 5, 0 ... Or count each child as 10 (two hands): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 - the same answer, faster.
Grandpa gives Anu eight ₹10 notes. How much money is it? Then he adds one ₹100 note. How much now?

Answer: ₹80. Then ₹180.

Count the tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. The tens digit goes up by 1 each time and the ones digit stays 0. Adding 100 makes the hundreds digit go up by 1: 80 becomes 180.
On one side of a street the houses are numbered 1, 3, 5, 7. What are the next three house numbers? Why?

Answer: 9, 11, 13. The rule is "add 2", so all the numbers are odd.

Jump on a number line from 1 in jumps of 2. We land only on odd numbers (ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). The other side of the street has the even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8. Ask: "Could 24 be on this side?" (No, 24 is even.)
Find the rule and the next two numbers: 7, 12, 17, 22, ...

Answer: The rule is +5. Next: 27, 32.

Look at the gap between each pair: 7 to 12 is 5, 12 to 17 is 5, 17 to 22 is 5. The rule is the gap that stays the same. Notice the ones digits go 7, 2, 7, 2 - this happens in every +5 sequence. Now let the child make up a +5 sequence starting from 3 (3, 8, 13, 18, 23 ...).
On a hundred chart, what number is just below 34? Just above it? Why?

Answer: Below 34 is 44. Above 34 is 24.

Each row of the hundred chart has 10 numbers, so going down one row adds 10 and going up takes away 10. The ones digit stays the same (4) and the tens digit changes. Colour the whole column: 4, 14, 24, 34 ... 94. Then ask for the numbers below and above 67 (77 and 57).
On a hundred chart, start at 1 and move diagonally down to the right: 1, 12, 23, 34 ... What is the rule? What is next?

Answer: The rule is +11. Next: 45, 56, 67, 78, 89, 100.

A diagonal step down-right is one row down (+10) and one step right (+1), so +11 each time. Both digits go up by one: 23, 34, 45. The other diagonal, down-left, is +10 - 1 = +9: 10, 19, 28, 37 ... Let the child colour both diagonals: they make an X.
Ravi has ₹50. He spends ₹5 every day on a snack. How much does he have left after each day, for 6 days?

Answer: 45, 40, 35, 30, 25, 20. After 6 days he has ₹20.

This is a "-5" sequence: counting back in 5s. Say it together while taking away one ₹5 coin each time. Ask: "After how many days will the money run out?" (10 days: 50 is ten 5s.)
Fill in the missing numbers: 35, 40, __, 50, __, 60.

Answer: 45 and 55.

First find the rule from two numbers next to each other: 35 to 40 is +5. Check it: 50 to 60 has one number between, 55, so the rule fits. Fill in 45 and 55. Always check the rule across the whole sequence.
Count on in 10s from 170: 170, 180, 190, ... What comes next? Count on in 100s from 250.

Answer: 170, 180, 190, 200, 210. In 100s: 250, 350, 450, 550 ...

After 190 comes 200, not "1100"! 19 tens and 1 more ten make 20 tens, which is 200. Show it with bundles of ten sticks: 10 tens make a hundred. For 100s only the hundreds digit changes: 2, 3, 4, 5 hundreds; the 50 stays the same.
The pattern 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 ... goes on. What is the 12th number? What is the 20th number?

Answer: The 12th number is 3. The 20th number is 2.

The pattern repeats every 3 numbers, so every 3rd, 6th, 9th, 12th ... number is 3 (counting in 3s). The 12th is 3. For the 20th: the 18th is 3 (18 is in the count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18), then the 19th is 1 and the 20th is 2. Let the child write the pattern out to check.

Look at the fruit bar graph in D6. Make up three questions that the graph can answer, and answer them.

Answer: For example: "Which fruit is liked least?" (grapes); "How many children answered?" (28); "How many more chose banana than apple?" (2).

A graph is made to answer questions. Give sentence starters: "Which is the most ...", "How many more ...", "How many altogether ...", "Is it true that ...". Also ask a question the graph CANNOT answer ("Which fruit does Ravi like?") - the graph does not show names.
Plan a survey: "What is our favourite snack?" What are the steps?

Answer: 1) Write the question. 2) Choose 4 or 5 choices (samosa, idli, fruit, biscuits, other). 3) Ask everyone and make a tally. 4) Count the tallies. 5) Draw a pictograph or bar graph. 6) Say what it tells us ("Samosa is the favourite").

Let the child do a real survey of family or classmates. Each person answers only once - tick names off a list. Talk about why the question must be clear ("favourite" means only one choice). This is how real scientists and newspapers collect data.

Who am I? "I am a 2-digit number. My tens digit is 4. My ones digit is 2 more than my tens digit."

Answer: 46.

Use one clue at a time. Clue 1: 2-digit, so 10 to 99. Clue 2: tens digit 4, so 40 to 49 - only ten numbers left. Clue 3: the ones digit is 4 + 2 = 6. So 46. Write the numbers 40-49 and cross them out as you go. Then let the child write a riddle for you.
In a number pyramid, each brick is the sum of the two bricks under it. Fill in the pyramid. [__] [__][__] [ 3][ 5][ 2]

Answer: Middle row: 8 and 7. Top: 15.

Show it with real bricks or boxes. 3 + 5 = 8 goes on top of 3 and 5; 5 + 2 = 7 goes on top of 5 and 2. Then 8 + 7 = 15 at the top. Then try one with a missing brick at the bottom: if the top is 20 and the middle bricks are 12 and 8, the child must think backwards (take away).
Ria is taller than Sonu. Sonu is taller than Tia. Who is the tallest? Who is the shortest?

Answer: Ria is the tallest and Tia is the shortest.

Draw three sticks: put Ria higher than Sonu, then Tia lower than Sonu. Order: Ria, Sonu, Tia. Point out: we never compared Ria and Tia directly, but we still KNOW Ria is taller, because Ria is taller than Sonu and Sonu is taller than Tia. Act it out with three children standing in order.
Amit, Bela and Chetan each like a different fruit: mango, apple or banana. Amit does not like mango. Bela likes banana. Who likes which fruit?

Answer: Amit: apple. Bela: banana. Chetan: mango.

Draw a grid: names down the side, fruits across the top. Tick Bela-banana, and cross out banana for the others. Cross out Amit-mango. Now Amit has only apple left: tick it. Chetan gets the last fruit, mango. A grid of ticks and crosses keeps our thinking tidy.
Is this true: "When you add two numbers, the answer is always bigger than both numbers"?

Answer: Sometimes true. 3 + 4 = 7 is bigger than both, but 6 + 0 = 6 is not bigger than 6.

To show a statement is NOT always true, we need just ONE example where it fails (a counter-example). Let the child try many sums, then give a hint: "What about adding 0?" Teach the three answers: always true, sometimes true, never true.
"If a number ends in 0, then it is even." 70 ends in 0. Is 70 even? Is every even number a number that ends in 0?

Answer: Yes, 70 is even. No - 12, 34 and 58 are even but do not end in 0.

An if-then rule works one way. Numbers ending in 0 are all even, but the even numbers also end in 2, 4, 6 or 8. Draw a big circle "even numbers" with a smaller circle inside "ends in 0". Everything in the small circle is in the big one, but not the other way round.
Which is the odd one out: 12, 18, 25, 30? Why?

Answer: 25, because it is the only odd number (the others are even). Another good answer: 30, because it is the only one in the 10s count.

There can be more than one right answer if the reason is true. Ask "Why?" every time - the reason is the maths. Let the child make their own odd-one-out puzzles for the family.
There are 3 coins that look the same, but one is a fake and is a little heavier. You may use a balance only ONCE. How can you find the fake?

Answer: Put one coin on each side and keep the third coin out. If one side goes down, that coin is the fake. If they balance, the coin you kept out is the fake.

Act it out with a toy balance (or a ruler on a pencil) and three coins, one with a little clay stuck under it. Talk through every possible result: left down, right down, or level. A good plan works in EVERY case. That is logical thinking.
I am thinking of a number from 1 to 20. You may ask questions that I answer only "yes" or "no". What is a clever first question?

Answer: "Is it more than 10?" - it cuts the numbers in half. With halving questions, you can always find the number in 5 questions or fewer.

Compare a slow question ("Is it 7?" - usually no, and only one number is crossed out) with a halving question (10 numbers crossed out). 20 -> 10 -> 5 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1: at most 5 questions. Play the game often and let the child be the one who asks.

The ones rod shows 3. How do you add 4 on the abacus?

Answer: 3 + 4 = 7. There is only 1 free lower bead, so bring down the upper bead (+5) and take away 1 lower bead (-1). The rod now shows 5 + 2 = 7.

4 and 1 are SMALL FRIENDS: they make 5. Adding 4 is the same as adding 5 and taking away 1. Say it as you move: "plus 4 is plus 5, minus 1." Practise every small-friend move: +4 = +5 -1, +3 = +5 -2, +2 = +5 -3, +1 = +5 -4.
The ones rod shows 6. How do you take away 3?

Answer: 6 - 3 = 3. There is only 1 lower bead to take, so take away the upper bead (-5) and push up 2 lower beads (+2). Now 3 lower beads show 3.

Taking away 3 is the same as taking away 5 and giving back 2, because 3 and 2 are small friends. Say: "minus 3 is minus 5, plus 2." Check: 6 - 5 = 1, 1 + 2 = 3.
The abacus shows 8. How do you add 7?

Answer: 8 + 7 = 15. 7 does not fit on the ones rod, so use its big friend 3: take away 3 from the ones rod (8 - 3 = 5), then add 1 bead on the tens rod (+10). The abacus shows 15.

3 and 7 are BIG FRIENDS: they make 10. Adding 7 is the same as adding 10 and taking away 3. Say: "plus 7 is minus 3, plus 10." Practise all big friends: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5.
The abacus shows 13. How do you take away 6?

Answer: 13 - 6 = 7. Take away 1 from the tens rod (-10) and add 4 to the ones rod (+4). The ones rod has 3, so adding 4 needs the small friend: +5 -1. The ones rod shows 7, the tens rod 0: 7.

Taking away 6 is the same as taking away 10 and giving back 4 (6 and 4 are big friends). Sometimes a big friend and a small friend are both needed - move slowly and say each step aloud. Check with a number line: 13 back 3 is 10, back 3 more is 7.
Work out in your head: 7 + 5 - 3 + 8.

Answer: 17.

Do one step at a time and say only the running answer: 7 + 5 = 12 (7 + 3 makes 10, and 2 more); 12 - 3 = 9; 9 + 8 = 17 (9 + 1 makes 10, and 7 more). Start with short chains of 3 numbers, said slowly, then make them longer and faster. Children can check on the abacus.
Add quickly: 4, 6, 3, 7, 5.

Answer: 25.

Look for pairs that make 10 (big friends): 4 + 6 = 10 and 3 + 7 = 10. That is 20, and 5 more is 25. Adding in any order gives the same total, so hunt for tens first. Then give lists like 8, 2, 9, 1, 6 (26).
Riya's grandfather puts ₹1 in her piggy bank in week 1 and doubles it every week: ₹2 in week 2, ₹4 in week 3. How much does he put in during week 7?

Answer: ₹64. (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

Doubling is adding a number to itself. Say the chain aloud: "1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64". For 16 + 16, double the tens (20) and double the ones (12): 32. For 32 + 32: 60 + 4 = 64. Doubling grows very fast! Practise doubles to 50 every day.
Close your eyes and imagine an abacus showing 23. Add 14 on your imaginary abacus. What do you see?

Answer: 37: the tens rod shows 3 (3 lower beads) and the ones rod shows 7 (upper bead and 2 lower beads).

First do it on a real abacus while saying each move: "tens rod: push up 1 more bead, 3; ones rod: 3 and 4 - small friend, down the 5, take away 1: 7." Then do it with fingers moving in the air over a picture of an abacus, then with eyes closed. This picture in the head is what makes abacus children so quick.
Add 45 + 38 on the abacus.

Answer: 83.

Set 45. Add the tens first: tens rod 4 + 3. There is no free lower bead, so small friend: +5 -2, and the tens rod shows 7. Now the ones: 5 + 8. 8 does not fit, so big friend: -2 +10. Taking 2 from 5 needs a small friend too (-5 +3), so the ones rod shows 3; then +10 makes the tens rod 8. Read: 83. Check mentally: 45 + 40 = 85, 85 - 2 = 83. Go slowly - this is a challenge question.

The newspaper says: "Six hundred four thousand fifty people visited the book fair." Write the number in numerals.

Answer: 604,050.

Write the thousands group first: "six hundred four thousand" gives 604 and a comma. The rest, "fifty", must fill THREE places after the comma: 050. So the number is 604,050. Every group after a comma always has exactly three digits, so fill empty places with 0. Common mistakes are 60,450 and 604,50. Check by reading your answer back aloud.
Now you try: write "three hundred thousand nine" in numerals.
The answer is 300,009.
Write 308,406 in expanded form.

Answer: 308,406 = 300,000 + 8,000 + 400 + 6.

Go along the number from the left and write what each digit is worth: 3 hundred thousands = 300,000, 0 ten thousands (skip), 8 thousands = 8,000, 4 hundreds = 400, 0 tens (skip), 6 ones = 6. Add them with plus signs. When we go back from expanded form to the number, we must put 0 in the ten thousands and tens places, or the number would shrink.
Now you try: which number is 90,000 + 700 + 5?
The answer is 90,705.
The meter on Papa's scooter shows 9,999 km. He rides 1 more km. What does the meter show now? What would it show after 99,999 km and after 999,999 km?

Answer: 10,000 km. After 99,999 comes 100,000, and after 999,999 comes 1,000,000 (one million).

Adding 1 to 9 ones makes 10 ones = 1 ten, so the ones become 0 and we carry into the tens. The tens were 9 too, so they become 0 and we carry again, and so on: every 9 rolls over to 0, like the wheels of a meter. So 9,999 + 1 = 10,000. The same happens with five nines and six nines: 99,999 + 1 = 100,000 and 999,999 + 1 = 1,000,000. Counting BACK undoes it: 10,000 - 1 = 9,999.

The meter on Papa's scooter shows 9,999 km. He rides 1 more km. What does the meter show now? What would it show after 99,999 km and after 999,999 km?

Now you try: what comes after 49,999?
The answer is 50,000.
Why is ten lakh the same as one million? How many lakhs make one crore?

Answer: 10 x 100,000 = 1,000,000, so ten lakh is one million. 100 lakh make one crore (1 crore = 10,000,000 = ten million).

Each place is 10 times the one to its right. One lakh is 100,000. Ten lakh is ten times that: 1,000,000, which the international system calls one million. Show it on the chart: the 1 moves one place left, from hundred thousands to millions. A crore is ten times ten lakh: 10 x 1,000,000 = 10,000,000. The Indian names go ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, ten lakhs, crores.
Now you try: how many thousands make one lakh?
The answer is 100.
In one month train A carried 208,745 passengers and train B carried 280,574 passengers. Which train carried more?

Answer: Train B. 280,574 > 208,745.

Both numbers have 6 digits, so compare digit by digit from the left. Hundred thousands: 2 and 2, the same. Ten thousands: 0 and 8. 8 is bigger, so 280,574 is bigger. We can stop here: the digits further to the right do not matter. If one number has MORE digits, it is bigger at once, as long as it does not start with 0.
Now you try: which is bigger, 99,999 or 100,000?
The answer is 100,000, it has more digits.
Four schools collected coins for charity: 45,210; 45,021; 54,120 and 45,201. Write the numbers from smallest to largest.

Answer: 45,021 < 45,201 < 45,210 < 54,120.

All four have 5 digits. Look at the first digit: 54,120 is the only one starting with 5, so it is the largest. The other three start with 45, so look at the hundreds: 0, 2, 2. 45,021 is the smallest. For 45,210 and 45,201, look at the tens: 1 and 0, so 45,201 comes first. Write the numbers one under the other with the digits lined up; it makes comparing much easier.
Now you try: order 30,303; 33,003; 30,033 from smallest to largest.
A counter shows 96,450. What is 1,000 more? 10,000 more? 1,000 less? 10,000 less?

Answer: 1,000 more: 97,450. 10,000 more: 106,450. 1,000 less: 95,450. 10,000 less: 86,450.

For 1,000 more or less, only the thousands digit changes by 1: 96,450 + 1,000 = 97,450. For 10,000 more or less, the ten thousands digit changes by 1. But 9 ten thousands plus 1 more ten thousand make 10 ten thousands = 1 hundred thousand, so the number grows to six digits: 96,450 + 10,000 = 106,450. Watch out for these roll-overs.
Now you try: what is 10,000 less than 1,000,000?
The answer is 990,000.
Use each of the digits 5, 0, 8, 2, 7 and 1 once. Make the greatest and the smallest 6-digit numbers.

Answer: Greatest: 875,210. Smallest: 102,578.

For the greatest number, put the biggest digit in the biggest place: 8, then 7, 5, 2, 1, 0. For the smallest, put the smallest digit first, but a 6-digit number cannot start with 0 (052,178 is really a 5-digit number). So start with the smallest digit that is not 0, which is 1, then put 0 next, then the rest in order: 102,578.
Now you try: make the greatest and smallest numbers from 4, 0, 9, 3, 6.
The answer is 96,430 and 30,469.
Arjun wrote "two hundred thousand forty" as 2,000,040. What went wrong? What is the right number?

Answer: The right number is 200,040. Arjun wrote one zero too many (his number is two million forty).

Break the words into groups: "two hundred thousand" is the thousands group 200, and "forty" is the ones group 040. So the number is 200,040. Arjun thought "two hundred" and "thousand" were separate, and put three zeros after 200 and then more. Always check: the thousands group has at most three digits. In the Indian way it is 2,00,040, two lakh forty.
Now you try: write "nine hundred nine thousand nine" in numerals.
The answer is 909,009.

85 is exactly halfway between 80 and 90. How do we round it? And 250 to the nearest 100? And 4,500 to the nearest 1000?

Answer: 85 -> 90, 250 -> 300, 4,500 -> 5,000. Halfway numbers round UP.

On the number line 85 is 5 steps from 80 and 5 steps from 90, so neither is nearer. Mathematicians agreed on a rule: when the deciding digit is 5, round up. This fits the pattern "0 to 4 down, 5 to 9 up": there are five digits in each group. The same rule works for every place: 250 has tens digit 5, so 300; 4,500 has hundreds digit 5, so 5,000.

Round 996 to the nearest 10.

Answer: 1,000.

The ones digit is 6, so round up: the tens digit must go up by 1. But the tens digit is 9, and 9 + 1 = 10 tens = 1 hundred. So the tens become 0 and 1 is carried to the hundreds, which are also 9: 9 + 1 = 10 hundreds = 1 thousand. The answer is 1,000. Check on a number line: 996 lies between 990 and 1,000, and it is 4 steps from 1,000, so 1,000 is right. A common mistake is to write 9100, squeezing 10 into the tens place.

An egg tray holds 6 eggs. How many eggs are in 7 trays?

Answer: 42 eggs. 7 x 6 = 42.

Use a fact you know: 7 x 5 = 35 (the 5 table is easy). 7 x 6 is one more group of 7: 35 + 7 = 42. Draw 7 rows of 6 dots and cover the last column with a finger: the rest is 7 x 5. The 6 table is always "the 5 table plus one more".

The 12 x 12 multiplication square has 144 facts. Why do we really have to learn only 78 of them?

Answer: Because a x b = b x a. Apart from the 12 squares (like 7 x 7), the facts come in pairs, so 132 facts are only 66 different ones. 66 + 12 = 78.

Turn an array of 3 rows of 8 through a quarter turn: it becomes 8 rows of 3, with the same dots. So 3 x 8 = 8 x 3. On the multiplication square, the numbers above the diagonal are a mirror of those below it. Colour the diagonal (the squares) and one half: that is all you need.

A shop has 3 boxes. Each box holds 4 packets, and each packet holds 5 pencils. How many pencils are there? Work it out in two ways.

Answer: 60 pencils. (3 x 4) x 5 = 12 x 5 = 60, or 3 x (4 x 5) = 3 x 20 = 60.

Way 1: first find the packets: 3 x 4 = 12 packets, then the pencils: 12 x 5 = 60. Way 2: first find the pencils in one box: 4 x 5 = 20, then 3 boxes: 3 x 20 = 60. The brackets show what we do first. Both ways give the same answer. This is the ASSOCIATIVE property: we may group three numbers either way.

Work out 5 x 9 x 2 and 4 x 17 x 25 in your head.

Answer: 5 x 9 x 2 = 90. 4 x 17 x 25 = 1,700.

Look for a pair that makes 10 or 100. 5 x 2 = 10, so swap and group: 5 x 9 x 2 = 9 x (5 x 2) = 9 x 10 = 90. In the second one, 4 x 25 = 100, so 4 x 17 x 25 = 17 x (4 x 25) = 17 x 100 = 1,700. Swapping (commutative) and regrouping (associative) together let us multiply in any order. Useful pairs: 2 x 5 = 10, 4 x 25 = 100, 2 x 50 = 100, 8 x 125 = 1,000.

Answer: 56. For example 7 x 8 = 7 x 4 + 7 x 4 = 28 + 28 = 56, or 7 x 8 = 5 x 8 + 2 x 8 = 40 + 16 = 56.

Split one of the numbers into parts whose facts you know. 8 = 4 + 4 gives double 28. Or split 7 = 5 + 2: 5 eights and 2 eights. Both ways give 56, which shows the answer is right. This is why the distributive property is so useful: no fact is ever really "lost".

Answer: 0 books: 5 x 0 = 0. And 1 x 347 = 347.

Five shelves with nothing on each shelf makes nothing: 5 x 0 = 0. This is the ZERO property: any number multiplied by 0 gives 0, even huge numbers: 0 x 5,678 = 0. One group of 347 is just 347: the IDENTITY property of 1. Children often mix these up with adding (where 5 + 0 = 5). Ask: "Is it groups of nothing, or nothing added?"

Answer: No. 8 - 3 = 5, but 3 - 8 cannot be done with whole numbers; 12 / 3 = 4, but 3 / 12 is not 4 (it is less than 1).

Use objects. From 8 sweets take away 3: 5 are left. From 3 sweets we cannot take away 8. Share 12 sweets among 3 children: 4 each. Share 3 sweets among 12 children: not even one each. So the order matters for subtraction and division. Only + and x are commutative.

The zeros inside a number hold places, so they move with the other digits. 4,080: 4 thousands, 0 hundreds, 8 tens, 0 ones. x 10: 4 ten thousands, 0 thousands, 8 hundreds, 0 tens and a new 0 ones: 40,800. Answer: 50 x 40 = 2,000, not 200.

5 x 4 = 20, and 10 x 10 = 100, so 50 x 40 = 20 x 100 = 2,000. Amma has 56 laddoos for the Diwali party. She shares them equally among 8 children. How many laddoos does each child get?

Answer: 7 laddoos each. 56 / 8 = 7.

This is sharing among 8. We do not need to deal out 56 laddoos one by one: we use the 8 times table. Ask, "8 times WHAT makes 56?" Say the 8 table: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 - that is 7 eights. So 7 x 8 = 56 and 56 / 8 = 7. Every multiplication fact gives us two division facts for free: 7 x 8 = 56 gives 56 / 8 = 7 and 56 / 7 = 8. Check: 8 children with 7 each is 8 x 7 = 56.

A shop packs eggs in trays of 12. How many trays are needed for 72 eggs?

Answer: 6 trays. 72 / 12 = 6.

This is grouping: we know the size of each group (12) and want HOW MANY groups. Count in 12s and keep a finger up for each tray: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72 - 6 fingers. So 6 x 12 = 72 and 72 / 12 = 6. A quicker way for the 12 table: 12 = 10 + 2, so 6 x 12 = 60 + 12 = 72. Learn the 11 and 12 tables as well as the others, because they give facts like 132 / 12 = 11 and 144 / 12 = 12.

At a school cricket tournament there are 132 players. Each team has 11 players. How many teams are there?

Answer: 12 teams. 132 / 11 = 12.

Think: "11 times what is 132?" The 11 table to 9 is easy (11, 22, ... 99). After that: 10 x 11 = 110, 11 x 11 = 121, 12 x 11 = 132. So 132 / 11 = 12. Check: 12 x 11 = 120 + 12 = 132. Big division facts are just the times tables read backwards.

The teacher has 47 pencils. She ties them in packs of 5. How many packs can she make? How many pencils are left over?

Answer: 9 packs, and 2 pencils are left over. 47 / 5 = 9 R 2.

Count in 5s but do not go past 47: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45 - that is 9 fives, and the next five (50) is too many. 9 x 5 = 45, and 47 - 45 = 2 are left. We write 47 / 5 = 9 R 2 and say "9 remainder 2". Always check: quotient x divisor + remainder = dividend: 9 x 5 + 2 = 45 + 2 = 47. A good question to ask is "Which is the biggest number in the 5 table that is not more than 47?"

Tina works out 29 / 4 and writes 6 R 5. What is wrong? What is the right answer?

Answer: The remainder 5 is bigger than the divisor 4, so she could have made one more group of 4. 29 / 4 = 7 R 1.

Tina's sum is not false (6 x 4 + 5 = 29), but it is not finished. If 5 are left and each group needs 4, we can make ONE more group and 1 is left: 7 groups and 1 left over. Rule: the remainder must always be SMALLER than the divisor. If it is not, add 1 to the quotient and take the divisor away from the remainder. Check: 7 x 4 + 1 = 28 + 1 = 29.

Divide the numbers 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28 by 7. What remainders do you get? Can you ever get a remainder of 7 or more?

Answer: 21 / 7 = 3, 22 / 7 = 3 R 1, 23 / 7 = 3 R 2, 24 / 7 = 3 R 3, 25 / 7 = 3 R 4, 26 / 7 = 3 R 5, 27 / 7 = 3 R 6, 28 / 7 = 4. The only remainders when dividing by 7 are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Never 7 or more.

Put the numbers in a row and watch the remainder grow by 1 each time: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 - and then, at 28, it goes back to 0 because 28 is the next number in the 7 table. The remainder is like a counter that starts again every 7 steps. So dividing by 7 has 7 possible remainders (0 to 6), dividing by 4 has 4 (0 to 3), and dividing by 12 has 12 (0 to 11).

Answer: 7 vans. 50 / 8 = 6 R 2, so 6 vans are full and 1 more van is needed for the last 2 children.

Work it out first: 6 x 8 = 48, and 50 - 48 = 2, so 50 / 8 = 6 R 2. But the answer to the STORY is not 6! Two children cannot be left at school, so they need another van. Here we ROUND UP: 6 + 1 = 7 vans. Ask the child, "What does the remainder 2 mean here?" (two children with no seat).

Nani shares 9 chapatis equally between 2 children. She cuts any left-over chapati into equal pieces. How much does each child get?

Answer: 4 and a half chapatis each. 9 / 2 = 4 R 1, and the 1 left over is cut into 2 halves.

Each child gets 4 whole chapatis (4 x 2 = 8), and 1 is left over. A chapati CAN be cut, so we do not throw it away: cut it into 2 equal halves and give one half to each child. So each gets 4 and 1/2. When the things can be cut (chapatis, cakes, ribbon), we can share the remainder as a FRACTION: remainder / divisor, here 1 out of 2 = 1/2. / comes before -, so 10 / 5 = 2 first, then 30 - 2 = 28. Neha worked left to right: 30 - 10 = 20, 20 / 5 = 4 - that would need brackets: (30 - 10) / 5 = 4. Careful: a cheap calculator that works out each step as you press the keys will ALSO show 4, because it goes left to right. Scientific calculators and computers follow the order of operations.

Is 7 a factor of 91?

Answer: Yes. 91 / 7 = 13 with no remainder, because 7 x 13 = 91.

To test whether a number is a factor, divide and look at the remainder: remainder 0 means YES, any other remainder means NO. 91 does not look like a 7-table number, but 70 + 21 = 91, which is 10 sevens + 3 sevens = 13 sevens. So 7 and 13 are a factor pair of 91.

Answer: ₹8, ₹16, ₹24, ₹32, ₹40, ₹48, ₹56, ₹64, ₹72, ₹80. They are the MULTIPLES of 8.

Each week adds another 8, so we are counting in 8s: these are the numbers in the 8 times table, 1 x 8, 2 x 8, 3 x 8 ... Multiples never stop: week 100 gives 800. Notice that 8 itself is the first multiple of 8, and every multiple of 8 is at least 8 (except 0).

Is 84 a multiple of 6? Is 95 a multiple of 4?

Answer: 84 is a multiple of 6 (6 x 14 = 84). 95 is not a multiple of 4 (95 / 4 = 23 R 3).

"Is 84 a multiple of 6?" is the same question as "Is 6 a factor of 84?" Divide: 84 / 6 = 14 exactly, so yes. 95 / 4 = 23 R 3, a remainder, so no. A quick check for 4: every multiple of 4 is even, and 95 is odd, so it cannot be one.

Meena has 12 pencils and 18 erasers. She wants to make gift bags that are all exactly the same, using ALL the pencils and erasers. What is the greatest number of bags she can make?

Answer: 6 bags, each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers. 6 is the HCF of 12 and 18.

The number of bags must divide 12 (so the pencils share equally) AND divide 18 (so the erasers share equally): it must be a COMMON FACTOR. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest is 6, the highest common factor. Each bag gets 12 / 6 = 2 pencils and 18 / 6 = 3 erasers.

Why does 16 have an odd number of factors, but 18 has an even number?

Answer: Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (5 factors, odd). Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 (6 factors, even). 16 is a square number, 4 x 4.

Factors usually come in PAIRS, which gives an even number. For 18: 1 x 18, 2 x 9, 3 x 6 - three pairs, 6 factors. For 16: 1 x 16, 2 x 8, 4 x 4. The last pair uses the SAME number twice, so 4 is counted only once: 5 factors. Only square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ...) have an odd number of factors.

Answer: 6 ways: 2 teams of 12, 3 of 8, 4 of 6, 6 of 4, 8 of 3, 12 of 2.

The number of teams must be a factor of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. We cannot have 1 team (not "at least 2 teams") or 24 teams (only 1 child in each), so the choices are 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 teams: 6 ways. Factors help whenever things must be shared or grouped with none left over.

Answer: 24 of each: 4 packs of samosas and 3 packs of chutney cups. 24 is the LCM of 6 and 8.

The number of samosas must be a multiple of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, ... The number of chutney cups must be a multiple of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, ... The first number in BOTH lists is 24. Why is 1 not a prime number?

Answer: A prime has exactly TWO different factors, 1 and itself. 1 has only ONE factor (1), so it is not prime. It is not composite either. 1 is in a group of its own.

Count the factors of the first few numbers: 1 has one factor; 2 has two (1, 2); 3 has two (1, 3); 4 has three (1, 2, 4). Primes are exactly the numbers with two factors, so 1 is left out. Mathematicians made this rule on purpose: it means every number breaks into primes in only ONE way (12 = 2 x 2 x 3). If 1 were prime, we could add "x 1" as many times as we liked.

The answer is 1, 2 and 3: neither, prime, composite.
Why is 2 the only even prime number?

Answer: Every even number can be divided by 2. So any even number bigger than 2 has at least three factors (1, 2 and itself) and is composite. 2 itself has only the factors 1 and 2, so it is prime.

Take any even number, say 38: 38 = 2 x 19, so 2 is a factor as well as 1 and 38. That is already three factors: composite. The only even number that escapes is 2 itself, because there "2" and "itself" are the same number. So after 2, every prime is odd - but careful, not every odd number is prime (9, 15, 21 ...).

Meena has 23 laddoos. She wants to pack them in equal boxes, with more than one box and more than one laddoo in each box. Can she?

Answer: No. 23 is prime, so its only factors are 1 and 23: either 1 box of 23 or 23 boxes of 1.

The number of boxes must be a factor of 23. Try 2, 3, 4, 5: 23 / 2 = 11 R 1, 23 / 3 = 7 R 2, 23 / 4 = 5 R 3, 23 / 5 = 4 R 3. We can stop there (5 x 5 = 25 is already bigger than 23). There is always a remainder, so it cannot be done. Prime numbers of things cannot be put in equal groups.

A school has 1,358 children. For the sports day march, they must walk in pairs. Can every child have a partner, with nobody left over?

Answer: Yes. 1,358 ends in 8, which is even, so 1,358 is divisible by 2 (1,358 / 2 = 679 pairs).

To test for 2 we only look at the LAST digit. Why? 1,358 is 1,350 and 8. Every ten can be split into 5 pairs, so 1,350 splits into pairs with none left over. Only the 8 ones are left to check, and 8 makes 4 pairs. So a number is divisible by 2 when its ones digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. These are the EVEN numbers. Common mistake: looking at the first digit (1 is odd, but that does not matter).

Papa wants to pay ₹2,345 for a school uniform using only ₹5 coins. Can he do it exactly? Can he do it with only ₹10 notes?

Answer: With ₹5 coins, yes: 2,345 ends in 5, so it is divisible by 5 (469 coins). With ₹10 notes, no: 2,345 does not end in 0.

Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 ... every number in the 5 times table ends in 5 or 0. Count in 10s: 10, 20, 30 ... every one ends in 0. Again only the last digit matters, because every ten is two 5s and one 10. Rule for 5: last digit 0 or 5. Rule for 10: last digit 0. A number that ends in 0 passes BOTH tests. Common mistake: saying 2,350 is not divisible by 5 because it does not end in 5; 0 counts too!

A cricket club has 5,346 tickets to give out equally to 9 schools. Can every school get the same number, with none left over?

Answer: Yes. 5 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 18 and 18 is divisible by 9. Each school gets 5,346 / 9 = 594 tickets.

The rule for 9 is like the rule for 3: add the digits. 5 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 18. If you are not sure about 18, add its digits again: 1 + 8 = 9. When the digit sum ends up as 9, the number is divisible by 9. When it ends up as 3 or 6, the number is divisible by 3 but not by 9. Look at this 4 by 4 square. Each number shows which L-shaped layer a dot belongs to. How does it show that 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16? 1 2 3 4 2 2 3 4 3 3 3 4 4 4 4 4

Answer: Layer 1 has 1 dot, layer 2 has 3, layer 3 has 5, layer 4 has 7. Together 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4^2.

Each time we make the square one bigger, we add an L-shape around two sides. The L for a 2 by 2 square adds 3 dots, for 3 by 3 adds 5, for 4 by 4 adds 7: always the next odd number. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2: 1 = 1^2, 1 + 3 = 4 = 2^2, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3^2. Let the child build it with bottle tops.

Picture a 12 by 12 square of dots. To make it 13 by 13, add a row of 12 along the top, and then a column of 13 down the side: 12 x 12 = 144 + 12 (new row) + 13 (new column, one longer) = 169 So to go from n^2 to the next square, add n and n + 1. This is why the gaps between squares (3, 5, 7, 9 ...) are odd numbers: 12 + 13 = 25 is odd. Check by multiplying: 13 x 13 = 130 + 39 = 169.

Why can we stop after crossing out the multiples of 7? Why don't we need to cross out multiples of 11?

Answer: Every multiple of 11 below 100 (22, 33, ... 99) is 11 times a number smaller than 10, so it was already crossed out. The first multiple of 11 with no smaller factor is 11 x 11 = 121, beyond 100.

Think of a number that is not prime, like 91 = 7 x 13. It has two factors; the smaller one is at most 10, because if both were more than 10 the number would be more than 10 x 10 = 100. So every non-prime up to 100 has a factor 2, 3, 5 or 7 (the primes up to 10), and those are exactly the steps we did. The rule: stop when the next prime x itself is bigger than the last number.

A UNIT fraction (numerator 1) is one single part: 1/6 is one of 6 equal slices of a pizza. Any other fraction is a count of unit fractions: 5/6 means five of those slices, just as 5 metres means five of the unit called a metre. So the denominator names the unit and the numerator counts them.

Why do we write 4 as IV and not IIII?

Answer: Because I placed before V means "one less than five": IV = 5 - 1 = 4. A symbol may not be repeated four times.

When a SMALLER symbol stands just before a BIGGER one, we subtract it. So IV = 4 and VI = 6: the I on the left takes one away, the I on the right adds one. In the same way IX = 10 - 1 = 9, and XI = 11. This SUBTRACTING rule keeps numerals short.

Rohan wrote 49 as IL (one less than fifty). Why is this wrong? What is the correct numeral?

Answer: Only six subtraction pairs are allowed, and IL is not one of them. 49 = 40 + 9 = XL + IX = XLIX.

The allowed pairs are IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD (400) and CM (900). I can only go before V and X; X only before L and C; C only before D and M. To write 49, split it by place value: 40 and 9. 40 = XL and 9 = IX, so 49 = XLIX. Check: 50 - 10 + 10 - 1 = 49.
What year is MCMXCIV?

Answer: 1994. M + CM + XC + IV = 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994.

Break the numeral into chunks from the left. M = 1000. Next C is before M, a bigger symbol, so CM is a pair: 900. Then X before C: XC = 90. Then I before V: IV = 4. Add the chunks: 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994. Underline each subtraction pair first; then everything else is just adding.
Sonu says VV = 10 and XXXX = 40. What rules has he broken?

Answer: V, L and D are never repeated (10 is X). No symbol is repeated more than three times (40 is XL).

Two fives make ten, and there is already a symbol for ten: X. In the same way LL would be C and DD would be M. For 40, four X's are too many; use the subtraction pair XL (50 - 10). So the numbers 1 to 10 go I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, and the tens go X, XX, XXX, XL, L, LX, LXX, LXXX, XC, C.

What is the biggest number you can write with Roman numerals using these rules? Can you write 0?

Answer: 3999 = MMMCMXCIX. There is no Roman numeral for 0.

M can be repeated only three times: MMM = 3000. Then the biggest hundreds is CM (900), the biggest tens XC (90) and the biggest ones IX (9): MMMCMXCIX = 3000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 3999. The Romans had no zero; that is why places with no value are simply left out, as in MMXXVI. Our Hindu-Arabic numerals, with the zero that came from India, make place value and calculation much easier.
India became independent in 1947. Write 1947 in Roman numerals. How many years is it from 1947 to 2026? Write that in Roman numerals too.

Answer: 1947 = MCMXLVII. 2026 - 1947 = 79 = LXXIX.

1947 = 1000 + 900 + 40 + 7 = M + CM + XL + VII = MCMXLVII. For the years in between, subtract in ordinary numbers: 2026 - 1947 = 79. Then 79 = 70 + 9 = LXX + IX = LXXIX. Also: 1950 (the Republic) = MCML.

Adding Roman numerals directly is very hard, so change them into our numbers first: XXIV = 24 and XVIII = 18. Add: 24 + 18 = 42. Change back: 42 = 40 + 2 = XL + II = XLII. This is why the place-value system we use today replaced Roman numerals for calculating.

Answer: 60 cm. P = 4 x 15 = 60 cm.

A square has 4 equal sides, so instead of 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 we multiply: 4 x 15 = 60 cm. Remember the unit: the answer is a length, 60 cm.

A triangular park has sides 5 m, 7 m and 9 m. What is its perimeter? What is the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with sides of 6 cm?

Answer: 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 m. The equilateral triangle: 3 x 6 = 18 cm.

For any triangle, add the three sides: 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 m. An equilateral triangle has three EQUAL sides, so multiply: 3 x 6 = 18 cm. Check: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18.

Honeycomb cells are regular hexagons. If each side is 4 mm, what is the perimeter of one cell? What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides of 7 cm?

Answer: Hexagon: 6 x 4 = 24 mm. Pentagon: 5 x 7 = 35 cm.

"Regular" means all sides are equal. A hexagon has 6 sides, so P = 6 x 4 = 24 mm. A pentagon has 5 sides, so P = 5 x 7 = 35 cm. The rule for any regular polygon is: number of sides x length of one side. Count the sides carefully on a drawing first.

A farmer's field has five straight sides of 12 m, 15 m, 9 m, 11 m and 13 m. How long is the path all round it?

Answer: 60 m. 12 + 15 + 9 + 11 + 13 = 60.

The sides are all different, so there is no short cut: add all five. Tick each side on the drawing as you add it. Look for easy pairs: 9 + 11 = 20 and 12 + 13 + 15 = 40, so the total is 20 + 40 = 60 m. A common mistake is to leave out one side.

The perimeter of a square is 36 cm. How long is each side?

Answer: 9 cm. 36 / 4 = 9.

A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 36 cm. Share 36 into 4 equal parts: 36 / 4 = 9 cm. Check: 4 x 9 = 36. Finding the side is the opposite of finding the perimeter, so we divide instead of multiply.

A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. Its length is 9 cm. What is its breadth?

Answer: 6 cm. 30 / 2 = 15, and 15 - 9 = 6.

The perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. Half of the perimeter is 1 length + 1 breadth: 30 / 2 = 15 cm. The length is 9, so the breadth is 15 - 9 = 6 cm. Check: 2 x (9 + 6) = 30. A common mistake is 30 - 9 = 21, forgetting that there are two lengths.
Now you try: perimeter 50 m, breadth 10 m.
The answer is length 15 m.
A triangle has a perimeter of 25 cm. Two sides are 8 cm and 10 cm. How long is the third side?

Answer: 7 cm. 25 - (8 + 10) = 25 - 18 = 7.

The three sides add up to 25. The two we know add up to 8 + 10 = 18. The missing side is what is left: 25 - 18 = 7 cm. Check: 8 + 10 + 7 = 25. The same idea works for any polygon: missing side = perimeter - the sum of the other sides.
Now you try: a quadrilateral with perimeter 40 cm and sides 12, 9 and 11 cm.
The answer is 8 cm.
A table top is 2 m long and 75 cm wide. What is its perimeter in centimetres, and in metres?

Answer: 550 cm = 5 m 50 cm = 5.5 m. 2 x (200 + 75) = 550.

The sides are in different units, so change them to the same unit first: 2 m = 200 cm. Then P = 2 x (200 + 75) = 2 x 275 = 550 cm. Since 100 cm = 1 m, 550 cm = 5 m 50 cm = 5.5 m. Adding 2 + 75 = 77 would be a big mistake.

Ravi added only two sides, 6 + 4 = 10: that is only half the way round. Meena multiplied, 6 x 4 = 24: that is the AREA (the number of 1 cm squares inside), not the perimeter. The perimeter is 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. Draw it on squared paper and walk round it with a finger.

Meera covers part of her floor with square tiles. Each # is one tile and each . is bare floor. How many tiles are there? What is the area of the tiled part? # # # # . # # # # . # # # # # . . . # #

Answer: Area = 15 square units (15 tiles).

Count row by row and write the number at the end of each row: row 1 has 4, row 2 has 4, row 3 has 5, row 4 has 2. Add: 4 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 15. Tick each square as you count so you never count one twice. The area is 15 square units, because 15 unit squares cover it.
On a squared page, Arjun draws this shape. # is a whole square and / is half a square (a square cut along its diagonal). What is its area? # # # / # # # # / # # /

Answer: 9 whole squares and 3 halves: 9 + 1 1/2 = 10 1/2 square units.

First count the whole squares: 3 + 4 + 2 = 9. Then count the half squares: 3. Two halves make one whole, so 3 halves = 1 whole and 1 half. Total 9 + 1 + 1/2 = 10 1/2 square units. A common mistake is to count every half as a whole square (that gives 12, too much). Pair the halves with a pencil line: "these two make one".
Why do we measure area with squares? Why not with circles, like one-rupee coins?

Answer: Squares fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, so they cover a shape exactly. Circles always leave gaps between them.

Let the child cover a notebook with coins: there are gaps between the coins, so the count does not tell us the true space. Then cover it with square paper tiles or sticky notes: they fit edge to edge. That is why the unit of area is a unit SQUARE. The size of the square must be the same every time, which is why we use 1 cm^2 or 1 m^2.
Now you try: can triangles cut from a square tile cover a floor without gaps?
The answer is yes, 2 halves make each square.
A photo is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Mark it into 1 cm squares. How many squares are there? Can you find it without counting one by one? # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # #

Answer: Area = 24 cm^2. There are 4 rows of 6 squares: 4 x 6 = 24.

Every row has the same number of squares: 6 (the length). There are 4 rows (the breadth). So instead of counting 24 squares we multiply: 4 rows x 6 = 24. This is why AREA OF A RECTANGLE = LENGTH x BREADTH. Write the unit: cm^2 (square centimetres), not cm. Draw a 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle on squared paper and check by counting that 5 x 3 = 15.
A classroom floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide. What is its area?

Answer: Area = 8 x 6 = 48 m^2.

Length x breadth = 8 m x 6 m = 48 m^2. Picture the floor marked into squares of 1 m by 1 m: 6 rows of 8 squares. Metres times metres gives SQUARE metres, m^2. For a big floor we use m^2, for a page we use cm^2. Ask: "Would the area of a floor in cm^2 be a big or a small number?" (very big: 1 m^2 = 100 x 100 = 10,000 cm^2).
A square handkerchief has sides of 9 cm. What is its area?

Answer: Area = 9 x 9 = 81 cm^2.

A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are equal, so area = side x side = 9 x 9 = 81 cm^2. A common mistake is 9 x 4 = 36 (that is the perimeter, in cm). Learn the square areas 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144 for sides 1 to 12 - they are the square numbers.
A vegetable garden has an area of 60 m^2. It is 12 m long. How wide is it?

Answer: Breadth = 60 / 12 = 5 m.

Area = length x breadth, so 12 x __ = 60. Ask: "12 times what is 60?" 12 x 5 = 60, so the breadth is 5 m. This is the same as 60 / 12 = 5. Check: 12 x 5 = 60. Draw a bar: 60 squares in rows of 12 make 5 rows. Watch the unit: the answer is a LENGTH, so it is 5 m, not 5 m^2.
Ravi says the area of a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm is 16 cm^2. What did he do wrong?

Answer: He found the perimeter: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. The area is 5 x 3 = 15 cm^2.

Draw the rectangle and mark it into squares: 3 rows of 5 = 15 squares. Then walk a finger round the edge: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. Perimeter is the FENCE around the field (cm); area is the GRASS inside (cm^2). Say "fence: add, grass: multiply". The numbers 15 and 16 are close here only by chance.

Priya traces a leaf on 1 cm squared paper. # means a square fully inside the leaf, o means a square that is half or more inside, . means less than half inside. Estimate the area of the leaf. . o o . o # # o # # # # o # # o . o . .

Answer: About 8 + 7 = 15 cm^2.

For a curved shape we cannot get the exact area by counting, so we ESTIMATE. Count the full squares: 8. Count the squares that are half or more inside: 7 - count each as 1. Leave out the squares that are less than half inside (they roughly make up for the bits we added). Estimate: 8 + 7 = 15 cm^2. Say "about 15 cm^2".
A verandah is 4 m long and 3 m wide. It is covered with square tiles of 1 m by 1 m. Each tile costs ₹250. How many tiles are needed and what is the cost?

Answer: Area = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2, so 12 tiles. Cost = 12 x ₹250 = ₹3,000.

Each tile covers 1 m^2, so the number of tiles is the area in m^2. Step 1: area = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2, 12 tiles. Step 2: cost = 12 x 250. Work it as 10 x 250 = 2,500 and 2 x 250 = 500, total ₹3,000. Draw the verandah as 3 rows of 4 tiles to check the 12.
Which has the bigger area: a rectangle 7 cm by 5 cm or a square of side 6 cm? By how much?

Answer: The square: 6 x 6 = 36 cm^2, the rectangle 7 x 5 = 35 cm^2. The square is bigger by 1 cm^2.

Find both areas, then compare. Rectangle: 7 x 5 = 35 cm^2. Square: 6 x 6 = 36 cm^2. 36 - 35 = 1 cm^2. Both shapes have the same perimeter (24 cm), but not the same area - we meet this idea again in topic 4.30. You cannot tell the bigger area by looking at the longest side.
Now you try: rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm or square of side 6 cm?
The answer is the same: 36 cm^2.
A rug is 4 m by 3 m. What happens to its area if the length is doubled? What if both the length and the breadth are doubled?

Answer: Length doubled: 8 x 3 = 24 m^2 (twice 12). Both doubled: 8 x 6 = 48 m^2 (4 times 12).

Draw it on squared paper. The first rug is 3 rows of 4 = 12 squares. Doubling the length puts a second copy beside it: 2 copies, 24 m^2. Doubling both makes 2 copies across and 2 copies down: 4 copies, 48 m^2. Many children think doubling both sides doubles the area - the picture shows it is 4 times.

Tanvi says, "If a rectangle has a bigger area, it must also have a bigger perimeter." Is she right?

Answer: No. A 10 cm by 1 cm strip has area 10 cm^2 and perimeter 22 cm. A 4 cm by 4 cm square has a bigger area (16 cm^2) but a smaller perimeter (16 cm).

To show a statement is wrong, one example that breaks it is enough (a counter-example). Work out both measures for each shape and put them in a table: strip 10 cm^2, 22 cm; square 16 cm^2, 16 cm. The square wins on area, the strip wins on perimeter. So area and perimeter are different measures and must each be worked out.
A school garden must have an area of 36 m^2 and whole-metre sides. Fencing costs ₹100 a metre. Which shape is cheapest to fence, and which is dearest?

Answer: Cheapest: 6 m by 6 m, perimeter 24 m, ₹2,400. Dearest: 36 m by 1 m, perimeter 74 m, ₹7,400.

Factor pairs of 36: 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9, 6 x 6. Perimeters: 74, 40, 30, 26, 24 m. The square uses the least fence. Cost = perimeter x ₹100: 24 x 100 = ₹2,400 and 74 x 100 = ₹7,400. Point out the pattern: as the sides get closer together, the perimeter gets smaller.
Rahul bends a 16 cm piece of wire into a rectangle with whole centimetre sides. List all the rectangles. Which one has the biggest area?

Answer: 7 x 1 (7 cm^2), 6 x 2 (12 cm^2), 5 x 3 (15 cm^2), 4 x 4 (16 cm^2). The 4 cm square has the biggest area.

Half of 16 is 8, so length + breadth = 8. Go down in order: 7 + 1, 6 + 2, 5 + 3, 4 + 4. Multiply for the areas: 7, 12, 15, 16. The wire (perimeter) is always 16 cm, but the space inside grows as the shape gets more square. Let the child bend a piece of string round pins on a board to see it.
Sita has 12 square tiles. She wants to arrange all of them into one rectangle. How many different rectangles can she make? Which has the shortest border?

Answer: Three: 1 x 12 (perimeter 26), 2 x 6 (perimeter 16) and 3 x 4 (perimeter 14). The 3 x 4 has the shortest border.

12 tiles: rows x tiles in a row = 12, so use the factor pairs 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. (4 x 3 is the 3 x 4 turned.) Every rectangle has area 12 square units. Perimeters: 2 x 13 = 26, 2 x 8 = 16, 2 x 7 = 14. With 7 tiles, only one rectangle is possible (1 x 7), because 7 is prime.
Two carpets both have a perimeter of 18 m. One is 7 m by 2 m; the other is 5 m by 4 m. Which carpet covers more floor?

Answer: The 5 m by 4 m carpet: 20 m^2 against 14 m^2 - 6 m^2 more.

Check the perimeters first: 2 x (7 + 2) = 18 and 2 x (5 + 4) = 18. Same border! Now the areas: 7 x 2 = 14 m^2 and 5 x 4 = 20 m^2. The same length of border can hold different amounts of floor. Ask: "Can you find a carpet with perimeter 18 m that covers even more?" (no whole-metre one: 4 + 5 is the closest pair to equal).
Now you try: perimeter 22 m: 9 m by 2 m or 6 m by 5 m?
The answer is 6 x 5 = 30 m^2, more than 18 m^2.
Can a rectangle with whole-number sides have a perimeter of 15 cm? Explain why.

Answer: No. Perimeter = 2 x (length + breadth), which is always an even number. 15 is odd.

Every length appears twice (top and bottom) and every breadth twice (left and right). A number used twice gives a double, and all doubles are even. So perimeters like 10, 12, 14 cm are possible, but 15 cm is not (with whole-number sides). With half-centimetres, like 4 1/2 cm by 3 cm, it can happen.
Now you try: can the perimeter be 30 cm?
The answer is yes, e.g. 10 x 5; half is 15.
A square of side 4 cm has area 16 cm^2 and perimeter 16 cm. Are the area and the perimeter equal?

Answer: No. The NUMBERS are equal, but 16 cm^2 is a space and 16 cm is a length - they cannot be compared. Only the numbers happen to match.

Change the unit to show it: in millimetres the square is 40 mm by 40 mm, area 1,600 mm^2 and perimeter 160 mm - no longer the same number! There is one more whole-number rectangle whose numbers match: 6 by 3 (area 18, perimeter 18). Let the child test other rectangles and see that the numbers usually differ.
Now you try: a 5 x 5 square: area and perimeter numbers?
The answer is 25 and 20.

For a rangoli competition, Kavya can decorate a square card of side 5 cm or a rectangular card 8 cm by 3 cm. She puts ribbon round the edge and paint inside. Which card needs more ribbon? Which needs more paint?

Answer: Ribbon (perimeter): square 20 cm, rectangle 22 cm - the rectangle needs more. Paint (area): square 25 cm^2, rectangle 24 cm^2 - the square needs more.

Ribbon goes round the edge, so find perimeters: 4 x 5 = 20 cm and 2 x (8 + 3) = 22 cm. Paint covers the inside, so find areas: 5 x 5 = 25 cm^2 and 8 x 3 = 24 cm^2. The shape with more paint has less ribbon! Always ask first: "Is this about the edge or about the inside?"

Sunil cuts the same room (from D1) DOWN instead of across. Does he get the same area?

Answer: Yes. Left part: 4 x 7 = 28 m^2. Right part: 5 x 4 = 20 m^2. Total 28 + 20 = 48 m^2 - the same.

Cut down along the step. The left rectangle is 4 m wide and the full height 7 m: 4 x 7 = 28. The right rectangle needs its width: the step is 9 - 4 = 5 m, and its height is 4 m: 5 x 4 = 20. Total 48 m^2. The area of the room does not change with the way you cut it, so doing it both ways is a good CHECK.
What is the perimeter of the L-shaped room in D1? Why is it the same as the perimeter of the 9 m by 7 m rectangle round it?

Answer: Perimeter = 4 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 9 + 7 = 32 m, and 2 x (9 + 7) = 32 m too.

First find every side: top 4, drop 3, step 5, right 4, bottom 9, left 7. Add them: 32 m. Now push the step up and out to the corner: the step (5 m) moves up to join the top, making 9 m, and the drop (3 m) moves right to join the right side, making 7 m. The edge is just as long, but now it is the rectangle 9 by 7. So for an L, perimeter = 2 x (bottom + left). But the AREA does change: 48 is less than 63.
A photo 20 cm by 15 cm is put in a frame that is 2 cm wide all round. What is the area of the frame?

Answer: Outside: 24 cm by 19 cm = 456 cm^2. Photo: 20 x 15 = 300 cm^2. Frame = 456 - 300 = 156 cm^2.

Add 2 cm on both sides: 20 + 4 = 24 and 15 + 4 = 19. Work out 24 x 19 with the area model: 24 x 20 = 480, minus 24 = 456. The photo is 300 cm^2. Frame = 456 - 300 = 156 cm^2. Draw it to see the frame as a border and the photo as the hole in the middle.
For the room in D1, Neha found 4 x 7 = 28 and 9 x 4 = 36, and added them to get 64 m^2. What went wrong?

Answer: Her two rectangles overlap: the bottom-left 4 m by 4 m square (16 m^2) was counted twice. 64 - 16 = 48 m^2, the correct area.

Draw her two rectangles on the plan in two colours. The tall left one (4 x 7) and the wide bottom one (9 x 4) share a corner piece 4 m by 4 m. The pieces we add must fit together like a jigsaw, with no piece used twice. Fix it by making the second rectangle only the part NOT yet covered: 5 x 4 = 20, and 28 + 20 = 48.
Now you try: an L with top 3, drop 2, step 4, right 3 (bottom 7, left 5). What is wrong with 3 x 5 + 7 x 3?
The answer is the 3 x 3 corner is counted twice; 15 + 12 = 27 m^2.

On squared paper, Aman draws a staircase shape. Each # is 1 cm^2. Find the area using rectangles, then check by counting. # # # . . . . . . # # # . . . . . . # # # # # # . . . # # # # # # . . . # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # # #

Answer: Rows in pairs: 3 x 2 + 6 x 2 + 9 x 2 = 6 + 12 + 18 = 36 cm^2.

Cut the staircase into three flat rectangles, one for each step. Top step: 3 wide, 2 tall: 6. Middle step: 6 wide, 2 tall: 12. Bottom step: 9 wide, 2 tall: 18. Total 36 cm^2. Counting row by row: 3 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 9 + 9 = 36. Or subtract: the full 9 by 6 rectangle is 54 cm^2, the empty part above the steps is 6 x 2 + 3 x 2 = 18 cm^2, and 54 - 18 = 36 cm^2.

How do you measure an angle with a protractor? The arm OA lies along the base line, on the side where the INNER scale starts at 0. The arm OB passes the mark that reads 65 on the inner scale and 115 on the outer scale. What is the angle?

Answer: Angle AOB = 65 degrees.

Steps on the board: (1) Put the small centre hole of the protractor exactly on the vertex O. (2) Turn the protractor so the base line lies along arm OA. (3) Find the 0 that sits on OA - here it is on the inner scale. (4) Follow the inner scale 10, 20, 30 ... up to where OB crosses: 65. The angle is 65 degrees. Look first: the angle is smaller than a right angle, so the answer must be less than 90 - 115 cannot be right. Reading the wrong scale is the most common mistake; the two numbers always add to 180 (65 + 115 = 180).
Riya measured an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle and wrote 140 degrees. What should it be?

Answer: 40 degrees. She read the wrong scale: 180 - 140 = 40.

Always ESTIMATE first. The angle is acute, so it is less than 90 degrees. At every mark the two scales add to 180, so the other number at her mark is 180 - 140 = 40. Teach the child to say "acute, so small number" or "obtuse, so big number" before writing the answer.
A round cake is cut from the centre into 3 pieces. Two of the angles at the centre are 120 degrees and 150 degrees. What is the third angle?

Answer: 90 degrees, because angles round a point add up to 360 degrees: 360 - 120 - 150 = 90.

A full turn round the centre is 360 degrees. Add the angles we know: 120 + 150 = 270. The rest is 360 - 270 = 90 degrees. So the third piece has a right angle at its tip. Check: 120 + 150 + 90 = 360.
Why is the angle between the hands at 1 o'clock 30 degrees? What is it at 3 o'clock?

Answer: 360 degrees / 12 = 30 degrees for each hour gap. At 3 o'clock the hands are 3 gaps apart: 3 x 30 = 90 degrees.

The 12 numbers are spread evenly round a full turn of 360 degrees. Each gap is 360 / 12 = 30 degrees. At 1 o'clock the minute hand is on 12 and the hour hand on 1: one gap, 30 degrees. At 3 o'clock: 3 gaps, 90 degrees, a right angle. At 6 o'clock: 6 gaps, 180 degrees, a straight line. Make a paper clock and mark 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees ...
At 7 o'clock, what angle do the hands make? There are two angles between the hands - find both.

Answer: Smaller angle: 5 gaps (from 7 on to 12) = 5 x 30 = 150 degrees. The other angle (the reflex angle) = 360 - 150 = 210 degrees.

Count the gaps the SHORT way round: from 7 to 12 going on is 5 gaps (7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 10 -> 11 -> 12), 5 x 30 = 150 degrees. Going the long way from 12 to 7 is 7 gaps, 7 x 30 = 210 degrees. Together they make a full turn: 150 + 210 = 360. When we say "the angle between the hands" we usually mean the smaller one.
A dancer spins a three-quarter turn clockwise. How many degrees is that? How many right angles?

Answer: 3/4 of 360 degrees = 270 degrees, which is 3 right angles.

A quarter turn is 90 degrees (one right angle), because 360 / 4 = 90. A three-quarter turn is 3 quarter turns: 3 x 90 = 270 degrees. Turn together in class: face the board, turn 90 degrees (face the window), another 90 degrees (180 degrees, face the back), another 90 degrees (270 degrees). A full turn is 4 x 90 = 360 degrees.
Fold a square paper corner in half through the corner. What angle do you get? Why?

Answer: 45 degrees, because folding the 90 degrees corner in half gives 90 / 2 = 45 degrees.

A square corner is 90 degrees. Folding it exactly in half splits it into two equal angles: 45 degrees + 45 degrees = 90 degrees. This 45 degrees is a useful benchmark: an angle that looks about half a right angle is about 45 degrees. Half of 45 degrees is about 22 degrees, and a right angle and a half is 90 + 45 = 135 degrees. Use these to estimate before measuring.
Now you try: what is two right angles and a half?
The answer is 90 + 90 + 45 = 225 degrees.
At 2 o'clock the hands make a 60 degrees angle. What is the reflex angle between the hands?

Answer: 360 - 60 = 300 degrees.

The two angles between the hands together make a full turn, 360 degrees. The small one is 2 gaps x 30 degrees = 60 degrees. The big one, going the long way round, is 360 - 60 = 300 degrees (or count 10 gaps: 10 x 30 = 300). A REFLEX angle is bigger than 180 degrees. Draw both angles and shade the reflex one.
A geometry box has two set squares. One has angles 45 degrees, 45 degrees, 90 degrees; the other has 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees. Which angles can you make by putting two corners side by side?

Answer: One corner from each set square: 45 + 30 = 75 degrees, 45 + 60 = 105 degrees, 90 + 30 = 120 degrees, 45 + 90 = 135 degrees, 90 + 60 = 150 degrees, 90 + 90 = 180 degrees.

Angles that sit side by side with a shared arm and the same vertex ADD. Take each corner of the first set square (45, 45, 90) with each corner of the second (30, 60, 90): 45 + 30 = 75, 45 + 60 = 105, 45 + 90 = 135, 90 + 30 = 120, 90 + 60 = 150, 90 + 90 = 180. You can also SUBTRACT by laying one corner on top of another: 45 - 30 = 15 degrees and 60 - 45 = 15 degrees. Let the child make each one and check with a protractor.

Now you try: which two corners make 105 degrees?
The answer is 45 degrees and 60 degrees.

Two roads cross like an X, but not at a right angle. Are the roads intersecting? Are they perpendicular?

Answer: They are intersecting (they cross at one point) but not perpendicular (the angle is not 90 degrees).

Every pair of perpendicular lines is intersecting, but not every intersecting pair is perpendicular. Draw a big X with a ruler and check the angle with the tester: two angles are acute and two are obtuse. The crossing point is the POINT OF INTERSECTION. Two straight lines can cross at most once.
In the capital letters E, H, L, T, N and Z (drawn with straight strokes), find parallel and perpendicular strokes.

Answer: E: 3 parallel horizontal strokes, all perpendicular to the vertical. H: 2 parallel verticals, the bar perpendicular to both. L: perpendicular, no parallel. T: perpendicular, no parallel. N: 2 parallel verticals, not perpendicular to the slant. Z: top and bottom parallel, the slant is not perpendicular.

Write the letters big on squared paper. For parallel, look for strokes going the same way (both across or both up); for perpendicular, look for square corners and check with the tester. In N and Z the slanting stroke makes acute and obtuse angles, not right angles.
How many straight lines can you draw through one point? Through two points? Through three points that are not in a line, joining them in pairs?

Answer: Through one point: endlessly many. Through two points: exactly one. Three points not in a line: 3 lines (AB, BC, CA), which make a triangle.

Put one dot on the board and draw lines through it in every direction - you never run out. Put two dots: only one ruler position joins them. For three dots, join each pair: AB, BC, CA. If the three points are in a line, only one line passes through all of them.
Can you measure a line segment? A ray? A line?

Answer: A segment: yes, it has two ends. A ray: no, it goes on for ever one way. A line: no, it goes on for ever both ways.

Measure seg AB with a ruler: put 0 on A and read at B. For a ray or a line there is no end to read, so there is no length. When we draw a ray or a line we draw only a piece of it, with arrows to show it continues.
Three straight roads cross each other so that no two are parallel and no three meet at the same place. How many crossings are there? What about 4 roads? 5 roads?

Answer: 3 roads: 3 crossings. 4 roads: 6. 5 roads: 10.

Add roads one at a time. Road 1 alone: 0 crossings. Road 2 crosses road 1: +1 (total 1). Road 3 crosses both: +2 (total 3). Road 4 crosses all three: +3 (total 6). Road 5: +4 (total 10). So the totals are 0, 1, 3, 6, 10 - the same numbers as the segments in D7. If two roads are parallel they do not cross, so there are fewer crossings.
Find parallel, perpendicular and intersecting lines in: the Indian flag, a window grill, a pair of scissors, a ladder, and a plus sign.

Answer: Flag: the stripes are parallel; the side edge is perpendicular to them. Window grill: bars parallel to each other, cross-bars perpendicular to them. Scissors: intersecting (not perpendicular). Ladder: the two long rails are parallel, the rungs are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the rails. Plus sign: perpendicular.
