Of the e-mails reaching an inbox, 40% are spam. The word "lottery" appears in 90% of spam e-mails and in 5% of genuine ones. An e-mail contains "lottery". Find the probability that it is spam, and explain the "prosecutor's fallacy".

Answer: P(spam | word) = 0.36 / (0.36 + 0.03) = 12/13 ~ 0.9231.

Branches: spam with the word 0.4 x 0.9 = 0.36; genuine with the word 0.6 x 0.05 = 0.03. P(word) = 0.39. The PROSECUTOR'S FALLACY confuses P(evidence | innocent) with P(innocent | evidence): "only 5% of genuine mails contain the word, so there is only a 5% chance this one is genuine" is WRONG; the correct value is 0.03/0.39 ~ 7.7%, and it would be much higher if spam were rarer. In court, "the chance of such a DNA match by accident is 1 in a million" does not mean "the chance the accused is innocent is 1 in a million": in a city of 10 million people about 10 would match.

Answer: Yes: P(car behind 1 | host opens 3) = 1/3 and P(car behind 2 | host opens 3) = 2/3.

Partition: car behind door 1, 2 or 3, priors 1/3 each. Likelihoods of "host opens door 3": if the car is behind 1, he chooses between 2 and 3 at random: 1/2; if behind 2, he MUST open 3: 1; if behind 3, he cannot open it: 0. P(opens 3) = 1/3 x 1/2 + 1/3 x 1 + 0 = 1/2. Posteriors: door 1: (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3; door 2: (1/3) / (1/2) = 2/3. The host's action carries information because it is constrained by where the car is. Intuition check: switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong, which happens 2/3 of the time. Common mistake: "two doors left, so 1/2 each" - that ignores the likelihoods.
Now you try: with 100 doors, the host opens 98 goat doors; P(win by switching)?
The answer is 99/100.

Of 4 keys exactly one opens a lock. Keys are tried one by one, without trying any key twice. Find the distribution of the number X of tries needed, and E(X). How does it change if the keys are tried at random WITH repetition?

Answer: Without repetition: P(X = 1) = P(X = 2) = P(X = 3) = P(X = 4) = 1/4, E(X) = 2.5. With repetition: P(X = n) = (3/4)^n^-^1(1/4) for n = 1, 2, 3, ..., E(X) = 4.

Without repetition: P(X = 2) = 3/4 x 1/3 = 1/4 (first key wrong, then the right one of the 3 left); P(X = 3) = 3/4 x 2/3 x 1/2 = 1/4, and so on: the right key is equally likely to be in any position. E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)/4 = 2.5. With repetition, every try succeeds with probability 1/4 independently, so X is GEOMETRIC with infinitely many values. E(X) = sum n(3/4)^n^-^1(1/4) = (1/4) x 1/(1 - 3/4)^2 = 4, using sum nr^n^-^1 = 1/(1 - r)^2 (differentiate the geometric series, 8.49). Remembering which keys failed saves 1.5 tries on average.
Now you try: probabilities of the geometric X must add to 1; check.
The answer is (1/4) / (1 - 3/4) = 1.

Explain which of these can reasonably be modelled by a Poisson distribution, and why. a) The number of misprints on a page of a novel. b) The number of heads in 20 tosses of a coin. c) The number of cars passing a toll plaza in a minute at 2 a.m. d) The number of customers entering a sweet shop per hour over a whole festival day. e) The number of goals scored in a football match. f) The number of students absent from a class of 40 during a flu outbreak.

Answer: a) yes b) no, binomial B(20, 0.5) c) yes d) no, the rate is not constant e) yes, approximately f) no, absences are not independent (and the maximum is 40).

Check the four conditions: events occur 1) singly, 2) at random, 3) INDEPENDENTLY and 4) at a CONSTANT average rate, with no fixed upper limit. a) Misprints are rare, random and independent: Poisson. b) There are exactly 20 trials with p = 0.5 and at most 20 heads: this is binomial, and p is not small. c) Late-night traffic is light and random at a steady rate: Poisson. d) The rate changes during the day (evening rush before the festival), so a single lambda does not fit; Poisson could work hour by hour with different lambda. e) Goals are fairly rare and random: a Poisson model with lambda ~ 2.5 is often used. f) Flu spreads from child to child, so absences are not independent. Common mistake: using Poisson just because something is "a count".
Now you try: the number of e-mails you receive between 3 a.m. and 4 a.m.
The answer is Poisson: random, independent, steady low rate.

Two typists prepare a school magazine. Anil makes errors at random at a mean rate of 1.5 per page and Bina at 2.5 per page, independently. Each types one page. Find the probability that the two pages together contain a) exactly 3 errors b) at most 1 error. c) What are the mean and variance of the DIFFERENCE A - B, and why is A - B not Poisson?

Answer: a) 0.1954 b) 0.0916 c) mean -1, variance 4; A - B can be negative.

Let A ~ Po(1.5), B ~ Po(2.5), independent. Then T = A + B ~ Po(1.5 + 2.5) = Po(4). P(T = 3) = e^(-4) x 4^3 / 3! = 0.1954 P(T <= 1) = e^(-4)(1 + 4) = 5e^(-4) = 0.0916 Check a) the long way: P(T = 3) = sum  P(A = i)P(B = 3 - i) over i = 0 to 3, which gives the same 0.1954. c) E(A - B) = 1.5 - 2.5 = -1 and Var(A - B) = Var A + Var B = 4 (variances ADD even for a difference). A Poisson variable is never negative and has mean = variance, so A - B is not Poisson. Common mistake: using Po(1.5 x 2.5) or forgetting the independence condition.

The heights of 100 randomly chosen Class 12 students have mean m = 162.4 cm. Assume sigma = 8 cm. a) Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean height mu of all Class 12 students. b) Explain what "95% confidence" means. c) How large a sample would halve the width?

Answer: a) 162.4 +/- 1.96 x 0.8 = (160.832, 163.968) cm b) see below c) n = 400.

Standard error SE = sigma/sqrtn = 8/10 = 0.8. For 95%, P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95, so the interval is m +/- 1.96 SE: margin = 1.96 x 0.8 = 1.568 interval = 162.4 - 1.568 to 162.4 + 1.568 = 160.832 to 163.968 (~ 160.8 to 164.0 cm) b) mu is fixed; the INTERVAL is random. If we took many samples of 100 and built an interval from each, about 95% of those intervals would contain mu. It is wrong to say "mu lies in this interval with probability 0.95". c) The width is 2 x 1.96 x sigma/sqrtn; halving it needs sqrtn doubled, so n = 4 x 100 = 400.

Use iso-profit lines to maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + 2y <= 10, 3x + y <= 15, x, y >= 0. Explain, using slopes, why the optimum is at the intersection of the two lines.

Answer: Z(max) = 24 at (4, 3).

Draw the lines 3x + 4y = 12 and 3x + 4y = 24; they are parallel with slope -3/4. Slide the line away from O: it leaves the region last at the corner (4, 3) (solve x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15: from the first x = 10 - 2y, so 30 - 6y + y = 15, y = 3, x = 4). Explain, using the pigeonhole principle: a) in any group of 13 students two were born in the same month b) in any group of 367 people two share a birthday c) a drawer has 10 black and 10 white socks; in the dark, how many must you take to be SURE of a matching pair, and how many to be sure of a BLACK pair?

Pigeonhole: more objects than boxes forces a box with two objects. a) 13 students, 12 months. b) 367 people, at most 366 possible birthdays (with 29 February). c) The boxes are the 2 colours: 3 socks in 2 colour-boxes must include two of one colour. Two socks are not enough (one black, one white). For a black pair think of the WORST case: you could pick all 10 white socks first, then need 2 black: 10 + 2 = 12. The general method: imagine an opponent making your draws as unlucky as possible, then add one. Common mistake: answering 2 for a pair, or 11 for a black pair.

Two opposite corner squares are removed from an 8 x 8 chessboard. Can the remaining 62 squares be covered by 31 dominoes (each covering two adjacent squares)? What if two squares of DIFFERENT colours are removed?

Answer: No: 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other remain, but each domino covers one black and one white. With two different colours removed, a tiling always exists (Gomory).

Colour the board as usual. Opposite corners have the SAME colour (say both white: (1, 1) and (8, 8), and 1 + 1 and 8 + 8 are both even). After removing them: 32 black, 30 white. A domino always covers one black and one white square, so 31 dominoes cover 31 of each: impossible. The invariant is "black covered - white covered = 0". Counting squares alone (62 is even) is not enough to decide. If one black and one white square are removed, a clever snake-shaped tour of the board shows a tiling always exists. Common mistake: trying many tilings by hand and concluding "I could not find one"; that is not a proof.
Now you try: can a 5 x 5 board with the centre removed be tiled?
The answer is colour count 12 and 12: the colour test allows it; yes, it can: tile the ring around the centre.

Find an INVARIANT: the PARITY of the sum of all numbers on the board. |a - b| has the same parity as a + b (they differ by 2 x min(a, b)), so replacing a and b by |a - b| changes the sum by an even number. At the start the sum is 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, odd; so the sum is always odd, and the final single number is odd, never 0. For 1 to 12 the sum is 78, even, so the last number is even. (A computer search over all move orders for 1 to 6, sum 21, finds only odd final values.) Common mistake: trying a few move orders and concluding it is impossible; the invariant gives a proof.

From a class of n students, count the ways to pick a committee (any size) AND a chairperson from it. Way 1: first choose the size k and the committee, C(n, k) ways, then the chair, k ways: total sum  k C(n, k). a) Prove that every tree with V vertices has E = V - 1 edges. b) 32 teams play a knockout cricket tournament (the loser of each match is out, no draws). How many matches are played? c) Which of these graphs are bipartite: a 6-cycle, a 7-cycle, a tree, the cube?

Answer: a) induction on V b) 31 c) the 6-cycle, every tree and the cube are bipartite; the 7-cycle is not.

a) A tree with V >= 2 has a leaf (an end of a longest path). Remove the leaf and its edge: still a tree, with one fewer vertex and one fewer edge. Repeat until one vertex and 0 edges remain: V - E = 1 at the end, and it never changed. b) Double counting: every match eliminates exactly one team, and 31 teams must be eliminated to leave a champion: 31 matches (no need to draw the bracket). The bracket is a tree! c) Try to 2-colour: an even cycle alternates colours; an odd cycle forces two neighbours with the same colour. A tree has no cycles at all. The cube: colour a vertex (x, y, z) by the parity of x + y + z. Common mistake: thinking "bipartite" means "has two parts that are not joined".
Now you try: a knockout with 20 teams (some get byes).
The answer is 19 matches.
